Commentary on Surah At-Talaq

His saying, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period (iddah), and count the waiting period, and fear Allah, your Lord. Do not expel them from their houses, nor should they leave, unless they commit a clear immorality. Those are the limits of Allah, and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has certainly wronged himself. You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter.﴾ ﴿So when they have reached their term, either retain them according to what is reasonable or part from them according to what is reasonable, and bring to witness two just men from among you and establish the testimony for Allah. That is instructed to whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever fears Allah – He will make for him a way out; ﴿And will provide for him from where he does not expect. He also narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: "No one swears by divorce or is made to swear by it except a hypocrite."

There is disagreement concerning the address to the Prophet (ﷺ) at the beginning, and then His saying after that, "you divorce." Some grammarians – related by az-Zahrawi – said: this is a shift from addressing an individual to addressing a group, and this exists. Others said: in addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), his community is also intended along with him, and therefore He said "you divorce." Others said: the meaning is, "O Prophet, say to them: when you divorce." Others said: it is like the way a great man says, "we did and we made," so the Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed with "you divorced" to show his honour. This is like His saying concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy: ﴿They are the ones who say﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7], when his statement is one that a group says. Likewise, the Prophet (ﷺ) in this matter is addressed with a plural address.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears to me in this is that they are two separate addresses: the Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed to draw attention to hearing the statement and receiving the command, then it was said to him: ﴿When you divorce﴾, meaning: you and your community. So His saying "When you divorce" is the beginning of a statement, as if He had begun the surah with it. The divorce of women is the dissolution of their marriage bond, and the forms of this and its categories are not specific to tafsir.

His saying: ﴿So divorce them at their waiting period﴾, meaning: at the time of its commencement, its duration, and its proximity to them. It is related from some of them, and from Ibn Umar, that both readings are from the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning of this verse is that no one should divorce his wife except during a purity in which he has not had intercourse with her. This is according to the school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others who said that "al-aqra'" (the term in the verse, usually rendered "periods") means the states of purity. Thus, according to them, the one divorcing divorces during a purity in which he has not touched her; the woman then observes the waiting period by it, then menstruates two menstrual periods, counting the purity that lies between them as part of the waiting period, then she remains in the third purity counting it as part of the waiting period; when she sees the first of the third menstruation she is released. Whoever says that "al-aqra'" means menstruation – and they are the Iraqis – says that "li-iddatihinna" means that she is divorced while pure, so she then begins three full menstrual periods; when she sees purity after the third, she is released. According to these, it is lighter whether he touched her during the purity of divorce or not. Likewise Malik says: "If he divorces in a purity in which he has touched her, the divorce takes effect." Divorcing a menstruating woman is not permissible, because the waiting period would be prolonged for her. It is said: rather she observes it, and even if the reason is prolongation, it should not be permissible even if she consents to it. The basis for this is the hadith of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "I divorced my wife while she was menstruating, and this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to Umar: 'Tell him to take her back, then keep her until she becomes pure, then she menstruates, then becomes pure, then he may divorce her if he wishes. Hudhayfah narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: "Divorce the woman at the beginning of her purity."

Then He commanded the counting of the waiting period, because of what follows from it of rulings concerning return, residence, inheritance, and other matters.

Then Allah the Exalted informed that they have more right to residence in the houses in which they were divorced, so He forbade expelling them and their leaving. The practice in this is that a divorced woman should not spend the night away from her house, nor be absent from it by day, except in necessity or for what is of no concern and is permissible conduct. This is for the preservation of lineage and the safeguarding of women. If the house is owned by the husband or rented from him, this is its ruling; if it is hers, then the rent is due from him. If she had enjoyed it during the marriage, then there are two opinions in the school as to whether it is obligatory for her to leave for the waiting period: the obligation, out of regard for the separation of the courtesy of marriage, and the exemption, because the waiting period arises from the cause of marriage.

This is also the view of ash-Sha'bi, Zayd ibn Aslam, Hammad, and al-Layth. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "illa an yafhishna 'alaykum" (unless they act indecently towards you). Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: immorality is all sins; so whenever she steals, or commits adultery, or engages in usury in trade or otherwise, her right to residence has lapsed. Ibn Umar and as-Suddi said: immorality is leaving the house in a manner of relocation; whenever she does that, her right to residence has lapsed. Qatadah also said: the meaning is: that they commit immorality by rebelling against the husband, so he divorces her because of that, and then she has no residence due. Some people said: whenever "fahisha" comes definite, it means adultery, and whenever it comes indefinite, it means sins; sometimes what is intended is the husband's bad treatment, and sometimes something else.

Asim read "mubayyanah" with a fatha on the doubled ya', saying: "bana al-amr" and "bayyantuhu" (I made it clear) on the intensive transitive form. The majority read it with a kasra, saying "bana al-amr" and "bayyana" with the same meaning, except that the doubling is for emphasis. From this is their saying: "The dawn has become clear (bayyana as-subh) to one who has two eyes."

His saying: ﴿And those are the limits of Allah﴾ refers to all His commands in this verse. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter﴾. Qatadah and others said: He means return (ar-raj'ah), i.e., count the waiting period, and comply with these commands which are agreed upon for your women, which preserve your lineages, and divorce according to the Sunnah; you will find a way out if you regret, for you do not know, perhaps the return will come afterwards. The word "ihdath" (bringing about) here is quite clear in direction; it is an expression for what is found of reconciliation. Some permitted that the meaning is a matter of abrogation, but that is far-fetched.

His saying: ﴿So when they have reached their term﴾ means the end of the period (al-qur'). "Retaining with kindness" means good companionship in spending and other matters; "parting with kindness" means paying the dowry, the provision (mut'ah), giving all rights, fulfilling conditions, and other things, according to each case. His saying: ﴿and bring to witness two just men from among you﴾ means: for the return; this is a condition for the validity of return, and the woman has the right to prevent the husband from herself until he calls witnesses. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: what is meant is for the return and for the divorce, because calling witnesses removes many problematic situations, and specifying the date of the witnessing is part of the witnessing. An-Nakha'i said: a just man is one in whom no suspicion appears; this is the view of the jurists. Justice in reality is one who fears none but Allah the Exalted. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and establish the testimony for Allah﴾ is a command to the witnesses. His saying the Exalted: ﴿That is instructed to whoever﴾ refers to the establishment of testimony, because all the details of rulings and matters revolve around the establishment of testimony.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And whoever fears Allah – He will make for him a way out﴾ ﴿And will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and many of the interpreters said: it concerns divorce, meaning: whoever does not exceed the Sunnah form of divorce to the divorce of three and other things, Allah will make for him a way out if he regrets, through the permitted return, and will provide him with what feeds his family and will widen things for him. Whoever does not fear Allah, perhaps he divorces irrevocably, then regrets, and has no way out, and his wife's provision ceases for him. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained something similar to this: he said to one who divorced three times: "You have not feared Allah the Exalted, so your wife has become irrevocably separated from you, and I see no way out for you." Ibn Abbas also said: the meaning of "He will make for him a way out" is that He will deliver him from the distresses of this world and the Hereafter. The wordings of the report of this story differ, but this is the meaning.

Some transmitters of reports said: "This verse was revealed concerning Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, for his son was captured and he was restricted, so he complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he commanded him to be mindful of Allah. Dawud ibn Hind read – and it is related from Abu Amr – "bali-ghun amruhu" with the nominative on "amr", the object being omitted, its estimate being: "bali-ghun amrahu ma sha'a" (He accomplishes His command however He wills). Dawud ibn Hind read – and it is related from Abu Amr – "bali-ghun amruhu" with the nominative on "amr", the object being omitted, its estimate being: "bali-ghun amrahu ma sha'a" (He accomplishes His command however He wills). **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 65, verses 4–7:**

The words of the Most High:

﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you have doubt, their waiting period is three months, and [likewise] those who have not menstruated. And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth. And whoever fears God, He will make for him ease in his affair.﴾ ﴿That is the command of God, which He has sent down to you. And whoever fears God, He will remove from him his misdeeds and magnify his reward.﴾ ﴿House them where you dwell, according to your means, and do not harm them so as to constrict them. And if they are pregnant, spend on them until they give birth. Then if they nurse for you, give them their wages, and confer with one another in kindness. But if you disagree, then another woman will nurse for him.﴾ ﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth, and whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what God has given him. God does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it. God will bring after hardship ease.﴾

"اللائِي" (alladhi): it is the plural of *dhat*, according to what Abu 'Ubayda related, but this is weak. What is well known among people is that it is the plural of *allati*, and it may also come as the plural of *li-dhi*.

The women who have despaired of menstruation are of several degrees. The first is the woman who is at the very beginning of her despair. Such a woman is brought up to the level of the Sunnah, and caution keeps her under the ruling of one who is not yet despairing, because she does not know whether the blood may return. The second is the woman whose blood has ceased because she has advanced in years and then been divorced, and whose customary bleeding has stopped, but who is among those who may rarely conceive. This is the one meant in the verse, according to one of the two interpretations of His words "if you have doubt." This is the view of those who make the doubt concern the matter of the year (i.e., the time of waiting), and it is the more apparent. The third is the woman who has become very old, so that it is certain she cannot conceive. She is not the one meant in the verse, because she has no doubt about her pregnancy. Rather, she falls under the ruling of the three months by consensus (ijma', i.e., the agreement of the scholars) as far as is known. In the verse, according to the interpretation of one who holds that His words "if you have doubt" mean that the ruling applies to those who have despaired, the matter is as follows. Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid related that some people among them, including Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may God be pleased with him, and Khallad ibn al-Nu'man, when they heard the words of God, "And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual periods" [al-Baqara 2:228], said: "O Messenger of God, what is the waiting period of one who has no menstrual period, either because of youth or because of old age?" Then this verse was revealed. One of them said: "Then what is the waiting period of the pregnant woman?" Then it was revealed: "And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth." The disagreement concerning the interpretation of "if you have doubt" has already been mentioned.

"أُولاتُ" is the plural of *dhat*. Most scholars hold that this verse includes both pregnant divorced women and pregnant women widowed by death. The proof is the hadith of Subay'a al-Aslamiyya, who said: "I was married to Sa'd ibn Khawla, and he died during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and I gave birth to my child about four months later." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "You are free to remarry," and he commanded her to marry. Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: "The shorter sura of Women was revealed after the longer one," meaning that His words "And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth" were revealed after His words "Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days" [al-Baqara 2:234]. Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "This [verse] concerns only divorced women. As for widows, the waiting period of the pregnant woman is the later of the two terms. If she gives birth before four months and ten days have passed, she must continue until the end of that period." The first view, that the term is merely [the birth], is the one held by the jurists. Al-Dahhak recited "ahmaluhunna" (their burdens) in the plural.

God commanded that divorced women be housed. There is no disagreement about this regarding a woman who has not been irrevocably divorced. As for the irrevocably divorced woman, Malik, may God have mercy on him, holds that she is entitled to housing because of the need to preserve lineage, but he does not hold that she is entitled to maintenance, because maintenance is in return for enjoyment (of the wife). This is also the view of al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, and Sulayman ibn Yasar. The Ashab al-Ra'y (the jurists of opinion) and al-Shura said: she is entitled to both housing and maintenance. A group of scholars said: she is entitled to neither housing nor maintenance.

"Al-wajd" means abundance in wealth. The vowelling of the *waw* as *damma*, *fatha*, or *kasra* all carry one meaning. The majority read "wujdikum" with *damma* on the *waw*, meaning the state of abundance. Al-A'raj, as reported by 'Isma, read "wajadakum" with *fatha* on the *waw*, and Abu 'Amr reported it from al-Hasan and Abu Haywa. Al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan and Ya'qub read it with *kasra* on the *waw*, and al-Mahdawi reported it from al-A'raj and 'Amr ibn Maymun.

As for the pregnant woman, there is no disagreement about the obligation to house and maintain her, whether she has been irrevocably divorced or not, because she is explicitly mentioned in the verse. The scholars of the community disagree on two views concerning the maintenance of a pregnant woman whose husband has died. One group prevents it, and another group makes it obligatory from the estate. Likewise, maintenance for a nursing mother is obligatory, namely her wage together with clothing and the other expenses which are set out in the books of jurisprudence.

As for His words "And confer with one another in kindness," they mean that each of you should urge the other toward good. There is no doubt that whoever urges good is quicker to do that good. Each should also accept what he is urged to do of what is kind. Acceptance and compliance is *ita'mara* (conferring/taking counsel). Al-Kisa'i said: "*i'tamiru*" means "consult one another." From this is His words: "Indeed the chiefs are conferring about you to kill you" [al-Qasas 28:20]. From this is also the line of Imru' al-Qays:

"... and what a man plots against him will overtake him."

As for His words "But if you disagree": it means that the woman has exceeded the limit of what would be a fair wage for nursing. Then the husband may hire another woman to nurse, in a manner that is gentler for him. However, if the infant will accept no one but his mother, she is then compelled to nurse him for a wage equal to her equivalent, taking into account the circumstances and wealth of herself and her husband. Then God specified for those of ample means that they should spend generously, and for those of straitened means that they should spend moderately, each according to his circumstances. This is justice between them, so that she is not neglected and he is not burdened with what he cannot bear.

The scholars differ concerning a man who is unable to maintain his wife. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Hurayra, Ibn al-Musayyib, and al-Hasan said: they are separated. Ashab al-Ra'y, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz, may God be pleased with him, and a group said: they are not separated. Then God gave hope of ease, to make it easier for souls and to console them.

The majority read "wa-yu'dhim" with *ya'* (ويُعْظِمْ), while al-A'mash read "wa-nu'dhim" with *nun* (وَنُعْظِمْ), and there is a difference of report from him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 65, verses 8–11:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿And how many a city rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We called it to a severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment. So it tasted the evil consequence of its affair, and the outcome of its affair was loss.﴾ ﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. So fear Allah, O people of understanding who have believed. Allah has sent down to you a reminder,﴾ ﴿a messenger reciting to you the clear verses of Allah, that He may bring out those who believed and did righteous deeds from darkness into light. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds—He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah has certainly perfected for him a provision.﴾

"Ka'ayyin" is the kaf of comparison (al-kaf al-jarr) entering upon "ayyin" (ay), and this is the reading of the majority. Ibn Kathir and 'Ubayd, from Abu 'Amr, read "wa-ka'inin" with a long vowel and a hamza, as the poet said:

*And many a friend in the valleys...*

Some readers read "wa-kayin" with the hamza eased (tashil al-hamza). In both of these readings there is a transposition (qalb), because the yā' comes before the alifs. "Al-'utuww" means refusing to heed commands and to accept.

As for His saying, "fa-hasabnaha" (so We called it to account): some of the exegetes said that the verse refers to the Hereafter, meaning: then there is the reckoning, the punishment, the tasting, and the loss of the outcome. Others said that this refers to this world, and the meaning of "hasabnaha hisaban shadidan" (We called it to a severe account) is that We did not overlook their slightest lapse, but held them to account for even the minutest of sins. Nafi', Abu Bakr and Ibn Dhakwan read "nukuran" with a damma on the kaf, while the rest read it with a sukun. This is the reading of 'Isa. His saying, "Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment," shows that it explains the reason for the loss of their outcome, and thus it is supported that the reckoning, punishment and tasting are in this world.

Then He, glory be to Him, urged the people of understanding toward taqwa as a warning. His saying, "those who believed," is a description of "people of understanding." Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "nudkhiluhu" with a nun, and likewise al-Mufaddal narrated from 'Asim, while the rest read it with a ya'. His saying, "Allah has sent down to you a reminder," "a messenger," people differed in the interpretation of this. A group of the exegetes said: what is meant by the two nouns is the Qur'an, and "rasulan" means "risalah" (message), and this exists in the speech of the Arabs. Others said: "rasulan" is an attribute, or like an attribute, of His saying "dhikran," so the meaning is "a reminder that is [accompanied by] a messenger." It was also said that "the messenger" is an explanation of "the reminder," as if it were a substitute for it. Others said: what is meant by both together is Muhammad, and the meaning is: possessor of a reminder, a messenger. Some skilled exegetes said: "dhikr" is one of the names of the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, and al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani argued with this in interpreting His saying, "No new reminder comes to them from their Lord" (al-Anbiya: 2). Some grammarians said: the meaning of the verse is: "a reminder" sent as "a messenger," so it is governed by a verb understood implicitly. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is permissible for "rasulan" to be an object of the verbal noun which is "dhikr."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The clearest of the sayings in my view is that "the reminder" refers to the Qur'an, and "the messenger" is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the meaning is: He sent a messenger. But brevity necessitated omitting the verb governing "rasul," and al-Suddi took this same approach.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr read "mubayyanat" with a fatha on the ya', while Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, al-Hasan, al-A'mash and 'Isa read it with a kasra. The rest of the verse is clear. The provision referred to is the provision of Paradise, for its permanence and abundance.

Some grammarians said: the meaning of the verse is: "a reminder" sent as "a messenger," so it is governed by a verb understood implicitly. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is permissible for "rasulan" to be an object of the verbal noun which is "dhikr."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The clearest of the sayings in my view is that "the reminder" refers to the Qur'an, and "the messenger" is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the meaning is: He sent a messenger. But brevity necessitated omitting the verb governing "rasul," and al-Suddi took this same approach.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr read "mubayyanat" with a fatha on the ya', while Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, al-Hasan, al-A'mash and 'Isa read it with a kasra. The rest of the verse is clear. The provision referred to is the provision of Paradise, for its permanence and abundance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 65, verse 12:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿It is Allah who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof. The command descends among them, that you may know that Allah is over all things competent and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge.﴾

There is no disagreement among the scholars that the heavens are seven, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿seven heavens in layers﴾ [Nuh: 15]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained their command in the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Sa'd (may Allah be pleased with him): "You have judged with the judgment of the King from above the seven ariqa," and the Sharia has affirmed this in more than one place. As for "the earth," the majority hold that it is seven earths, and this is the apparent meaning of this verse, and that the likeness is only in number. They cite the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever usurps a span of land, it will be hung around his neck from seven earths," along with other reports that have come concerning this. It is also related from a group of scholars that they said: the earth is one, and it is similar to each heaven individually in the height of its body, and in that it contains a world that worships, just as every heaven contains a world that worships. (p-337)

The majority read "mithlahunna" (مِثْلَهُنَّ) with the fatha (accusative), and 'Asim read "mithluhunna" (مِثْلُهُنَّ) with the damma (nominative). "Al-amr" (الأمْرُ) here means the revelation and all that Allah the Exalted commands, whether rational or non-rational, for the winds, the clouds and others are all commanded. The rest of the surah is an exhortation to the monotheism of Allah the Exalted.

As for His saying, the Exalted: (Indeed Allah is over all things competent), its general meaning is intended as particular. As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾, it is general in its unrestricted sense.

The tafsir of the surah of [al-Talaq] is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
